verses.text: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the captivity were building a temple to Yahweh, the God of Israel;

they came near to Zerubbabel, and to the heads of fathers’ households, and said to them, “Let us build with you; for we seek your God, as you do; and we have been sacrificing to him since the days of Esar Haddon king of Assyria, who brought us up here.”

But Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers’ households of Israel, said to them, “You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we ourselves together will build to Yahweh, the God of Israel, as king Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us.”
Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building.
They hired counselors against them, to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.
In the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, wrote they an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.

In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of his companions, wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter was written in Syrian, and delivered in the Syrian language.
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows,

then Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions, the Dinaites, and the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Shushanchites, the Dehaites, the Elamites,
and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar brought over, and set in the city of Samaria, and in the rest of the country beyond the River, and so forth, wrote.
This is the copy of the letter that they sent: To King Artaxerxes, From your servants the men beyond the River.
Be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you have come to us to Jerusalem. They are building the rebellious and bad city, and have finished the walls, and repaired the foundations.
Be it known now to the king that if this city is built and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and in the end it will be hurtful to the kings.
Now because we eat the salt of the palace, and it is not appropriate for us to see the king’s dishonor, therefore we have sent and informed the king,

that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will see in the book of the records, and know that this city is a rebellious city, and hurtful to kings and provinces, and that they have started rebellions within it in the past. That is why this city was destroyed.
We inform the king that, if this city is built and the walls finished, then you will have no possession beyond the River.
Then the king sent an answer to Rehum the chancellor, and to Shimshai the scribe, and to the rest of their companions who live in Samaria, and in the rest of the country beyond the River: Peace.
The letter which you sent to us has been plainly read before me.
I decreed, and search has been made, and it was found that this city has made insurrection against kings in the past, and that rebellion and revolts have been made in it.
There have also been mighty kings over Jerusalem, who have ruled over all the country beyond the River; and tribute, custom, and toll, was paid to them.
Make a decree now to cause these men to cease, and that this city not be built, until a decree is made by me.
Be careful that you not be slack doing so. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings?
Then when the copy of king Artaxerxes’ letter was read before Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went in haste to Jerusalem to the Jews, and made them to cease by force of arms.
Then work stopped on God’s house which is at Jerusalem. It stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

footnotes.content: The enemies of Judah and Benjamin learned about the temple building and moved quickly to interfere. Trouble often finds the faithful when they're doing the Lord's work—this is the way of the world, but never a sign of the Lord's absence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The adversaries came offering partnership, claiming they too worshipped the God of Israel. How easy it would have been to accept help; how wise that Zerubbabel saw through flattery to the false heart behind it. The Lord's work must not compromise its holiness through wavering companions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zerubbabel and Jeshua spoke firmly: 'You have nothing to do with us.' They held the line not from pride but from obedience to King Cyrus's command and the Lord's covenant. Standing alone is harder than going along, but it is where faith lives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rejection turned to persecution. The people of the land 'weakened the hands' of Judah's workers—a phrase capturing the weight of discouragement, the soul's exhaustion under sustained opposition. Yet the Lord was working underneath, even when His people's hands grew weary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Year after year, through Cyrus's reign and into Darius's, the enemies hired counselors to thwart the work. Long opposition tests whether our dedication is born of genuine faith or merely passing fervor. The faithful remnant endured because their eyes were on the Lord, not the timeline.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A new king, Ahasuerus, began his reign, and immediately an accusation was written against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. With each change of power, the opposition shifted shape. The faithful know that earthly kingdoms rise and fall, but the Lord's kingdom stands forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Under Artaxerxes, the letter was written in Aramaic, the diplomatic language of empire. The enemies knew how to work the system. Yet we see God's providence: this very letter, preserved for us, becomes a record of His faithfulness through opposition.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe put their names to the complaint. Men who fancied themselves clever, wielding the power of written word and royal office. The Lord does not fear such instruments; He turns them toward His own purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A list of tribes and peoples—Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, and more—joined the accusation. The nations born of Babylon's deportations, now settled in Samaria, united against Judah's restoration. Division has always been easier to forge than the unity the Lord builds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Osnappar's colonists, the great and noble peoples he had settled throughout the land 'beyond the River,' now added their voices to the complaint. Might and numbers do not measure the truth; they only measure earthly power, which the Lord permits and overrules.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The letter began: 'To King Artaxerxes, From your servants the men beyond the River.' How swift and smooth such appeals sound—the language of subordinates speaking to power. But the Lord hears not the eloquence of men but the cry of His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The accusers painted the Jews' rebuilding as rebellion: 'rebellious and bad city,' walls 'finished,' foundations 'repaired.' They distorted what was holy into what sounded dangerous. This is the enemy's old trick—make faithfulness sound like sedition, and righteousness sound like threat.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The accusers warned: a rebuilt city would refuse to pay tribute and hurt the king. They wrapped their malice in the language of loyalty—the deepest deception. How often does opposition hide behind concern for order, when it is only fear of the Lord's people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'We eat the salt of the palace'—these men claimed loyalty by sharing the king's table. Yet they betrayed that loyalty by turning against those the king had freed. Privilege without principle is merely appetite dressed as duty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The accusers appealed to the historical record: Jerusalem 'has started rebellions within it in the past' and 'was destroyed' for it. They twisted history as propaganda. Yet the Lord permitted even this record to reach the king's ears—part of His larger story of restoration, not ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'If this city is built… you will have no possession beyond the River.' The accusers painted themselves as protectors of the empire. But the Lord alone holds dominion over all lands; the accusers merely borrowed earthly authority for a moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king replied to Rehum and Shimshai with a single word: 'Peace.' Yet peace, here, was the peace of indifference—a king granting what those who fear God's people demand. The Lord's work has always proceeded under the shadow of earthly powers; He is not surprised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'The letter which you sent to us has been plainly read before me.' Artaxerxes acknowledged the accusation. He would hear the case, weigh it, and render judgment. The Lord permits earthly rulers their stage, but the final judgment is His alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king searched the records and confirmed: Jerusalem 'has made insurrection against kings in the past' and 'rebellion and revolts have been made in it.' History condemned the city in the eyes of power. Yet the Lord was preparing to rebuild what earthly power had destroyed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mighty kings before had ruled Jerusalem and collected tribute. Artaxerxes rehearsed the ancient grandeur of the city. Even his acknowledgment of Jerusalem's former strength became a reason to fear its restoration. How easily power misjudges what it cannot control.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Make a decree now to cause these men to cease, and that this city not be built, until a decree is made by me.' The king issued a stop-work order. The builders' hands fell still. This is the valley the faithful walk sometimes—obedience halted, the work suspended, waiting for the Lord's timing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Be careful that you not be slack doing so. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings?' Artaxerxes urged vigilance against the Jews. Yet what earthly king calls 'damage' is often the Lord's hand reshaping what must be remade. The king's concern cannot stop what God intends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the letter was read, Rehum and his companions moved swiftly to Jerusalem 'in haste' and 'made them to cease by force of arms.' Opposition turned to force; enforcement was swift and certain. The faithful have endured such moments—work halted by earthly power, yet faith unshaken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Work on the temple stopped entirely, frozen 'until the second year of the reign of Darius.' Readers today hear an echo in this: how often the Lord's work seems stalled by forces we cannot move, only to resume in His time, not ours. Waiting teaches us that the building belongs to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
